html:
This bar covers Iran from the rise of the Qajar dynasty, through the Pahlavi shahs, to the Islamic Republic that has ruled since 1979.

The Qajars (1789 to 1925). A Turkmen tribe whose chief, Agha Mohammad Khan, reunited Iran and made Tehran the capital. In two wars Russia took the Caucasus from them, by treaties in 1813 and 1828. Britain and Russia then competed for influence and concessions, and the shahs sold monopolies to foreigners to pay their debts. A great famine struck in 1870 to 1872. The Constitutional Revolution of 1905 to 1911 won Iran a parliament. Oil was found in 1908, and the British-owned Anglo-Persian Oil Company took most of the profits.

The Pahlavis (1925 to 1979). Reza Khan, an army officer, seized power in 1921 and made himself shah in 1925. He built roads, a railway and schools, and forced Western dress. Britain and the Soviet Union occupied Iran in 1941 and replaced him with his son, Mohammad Reza. When Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh nationalised the oil industry, a coup backed by the United States and Britain removed him in 1953. The shah's White Revolution of 1963 brought land reform, but his rule grew more repressive.

The Islamic Republic (1979 on). The Iranian Revolution of 1979 ended the monarchy, and Khomeini became Supreme Leader under a new constitution that puts Shia clergy above elected bodies. Iraq invaded in 1980, and the war lasted eight years. Since then Iran has lived with sanctions, disputes over its nuclear programme, and repeated waves of protest. It remains a founding member of OPEC.
sum: This bar covers Iran from the rise of the Qajar dynasty, through the Pahlavi shahs, to the Islamic Republic that has ruled since 1979.
